title: Why the Books Rest
hookLine: night seven: the fierce Kalaratri arrives, and in many homes the schoolbooks are laid before Saraswati to rest
carry: learning is sacred: the book is Saraswati's
tomorrow: why do grown-ups wash little girls' feet?

lines: THE SEVENTH NAME IS NOT GENTLE.
cards: A schoolbook, a pen, a harmonium, a child's slate.

In some homes, around this point in Navaratri, they're stacked together in front of an image of Saraswati, the goddess of learning, music and speech, and decorated with a little sandal paste and a flower.

Then nobody touches them: no homework from those books, no practice on that instrument, until the festival is over. In the three-by-three way of keeping the festival, Saraswati's nights begin about now.
But the seventh name in the Kavacha's list is not gentle at all.

teach.b: Her name is Kalaratri. You can hear ratri in it, night, the same word that's in Navaratri. In paintings of this night she's black as a moonless sky, hair loose and wild, breath like fire, sometimes riding a donkey.

teach.h: SHUBHANKARI: FIERCE, AND SHE DOES GOOD.
teach.b: And yet devotees who keep the nine forms give her a second name, Shubhankari, the one who does good. Hindus come back to that idea again and again: the fierce form of the goddess is the protecting one.
Her terror points at whatever would harm her children, never at them. Now the books.
In homes that keep it, especially in the South, the last days of Navaratri turn to Saraswati, and the tools of learning are set before her: schoolbooks, pens, a harmonium, a child's slate.
The reason is a belief most Hindu kids learn early.
Knowledge isn't just information. It belongs to Saraswati; it's a form of the goddess herself.

teach.h: DROP A BOOK, TOUCH IT TO YOUR FOREHEAD.
teach.b: That's why a Hindu child who steps on a book, or drops one, picks it up and touches it to the forehead, a small sorry. For these days the books rest.

Then on the tenth day they're picked up with a blessing, and in Kerala and other places small children write their first letters, often traced in a plate of rice, a rite called vidyarambham, the beginning of learning.
So night seven sets two faces of one goddess side by side: the dark one who guards, and the bright one who teaches.

teach.h: LEARNING IS SOMETHING YOU BOW TO.
teach.b: Learning isn't only something you use. It's something you bow to.

how: In many Hindu homes, especially in South India, books, pens and instruments are placed before Saraswati in the last days of Navaratri and not used until Vijayadashami, when they are taken up with a blessing and small children begin to write (vidyarambham); a dropped book is touched to the forehead. Where the nine forms are kept, the seventh night honors Kalaratri.

practice: Pick up a book near you, any book, or the phone you read on, and hold it for a moment the way a Hindu child does after dropping one: touch it lightly to your forehead. Bring to mind one thing you're learning right now.
If you pray, you can say Saraswati's name, or pray to God in your own words, and ask for a clear mind. If you don't, simply thank the teachers who got you here.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Kalaratri, the seventh of the nine forms named in the Devi Kavacha; ratri means night.
